Keywords: vertical slice, end to end, mvp, increment, small pr, walking skeleton
Description: Deliver one narrow path through every layer before widening.
When to Use: New features with several layers or many criteria.
How to Apply: Pick one acceptance criterion; implement just enough UI, API, logic and storage for it; ship and verify; add the next slice.
Risks: Slices that are thin in one layer only; skipping the error path of the slice.

Keywords: spike, prototype, proof of concept, poc, experiment, unknown, research, try out
Description: A time-boxed throwaway experiment to answer one technical question.
When to Use: A risky unknown (library, API, performance, feasibility) blocks the plan.
How to Apply: Write the question; set a time box; build the smallest thing that answers it; record the answer; delete or rewrite the code properly.

Keywords: feature flag, toggle, dark launch, gradual rollout, kill switch, canary
Description: Ship code switched off and turn it on separately from deploying.
When to Use: Risky or incomplete changes, gradual rollouts, quick rollback.
How to Apply: Wrap the new path behind a flag with the old path as default; test both; roll out gradually; remove the flag and old path when done.
Risks: Flags that are never removed; untested flag combinations.

Keywords: make the change easy, preparatory, refactor first, clean before change
Description: First make the change easy (which may be hard), then make the easy change.
When to Use: The feature or fix would be awkward in the current structure.
How to Apply: Refactor with behavior unchanged and tests green; commit; then make the actual change in a separate commit.
Risks: Refactoring far beyond what the change needs.

Keywords: mikado, dependency graph, large refactor, prerequisites, try and revert
Description: Try the goal change, note what breaks, revert, and fix prerequisites first, building a graph of steps.
When to Use: Large refactors where every change seems to break something else.
How to Apply: Attempt the goal; write the breakages as prerequisite nodes; revert; repeat on the leaves; do the leaves first with green tests.
Risks: Not reverting between attempts, leaving the code broken.

Keywords: seam, legacy code, dependency injection, test harness, break dependency, untestable
Description: A place where behavior can change without editing that place, used to get legacy code under test.
When to Use: Code that cannot be tested because of hard-wired dependencies.
How to Apply: Introduce a parameter, interface or wrapper at the dependency; pass a fake in tests; keep production wiring unchanged.
Risks: Adding seams everywhere instead of where tests need them.

Keywords: expand contract, parallel change, backward compatible, deprecate, api change, schema change
Description: Change an interface in three steps: add the new one, migrate callers, remove the old one.
When to Use: Changing public APIs, schemas or contracts used by others.
How to Apply: Expand: add the new form alongside the old. Migrate: move callers over, one at a time. Contract: remove the old form once nothing uses it.
Risks: Never finishing the contract step; data written in both formats getting out of sync.

Keywords: strangler, incremental rewrite, legacy replacement, route traffic, replace system
Description: Replace a system piece by piece, routing more traffic to the new one until the old can be removed.
When to Use: Replacing a legacy system or module without a big-bang cutover.
How to Apply: Put a routing layer in front; move one capability at a time to the new implementation; verify; remove the old capability.
Risks: Running two systems forever; inconsistent data between them.

Keywords: branch by abstraction, interface, swap implementation, abstraction layer, trunk based
Description: Introduce an abstraction over the code to replace, build the new implementation behind it, then switch.
When to Use: Large replacements done on the main branch without long-lived branches.
How to Apply: Add an interface used by all callers; keep the old implementation behind it; build the new one; switch (optionally by flag); delete the old one.
Risks: An abstraction that leaks details of the old implementation.

Keywords: codemod, ast, automated refactor, ide refactor, rename symbol, jscodeshift, comby, sed
Description: Use IDE refactorings or AST-based scripts for repetitive, mechanical edits.
When to Use: Renames, API migrations and patterns repeated across many files.
How to Apply: Write or pick the transformation; run it on a small sample; review; run on everything; run tests; commit the codemod separately from manual edits.
Risks: Regex edits that change strings or comments by accident.

Keywords: dead code, unused, delete, remove, cleanup, unreachable
When to Use: Refactors and migrations that leave old paths behind.
How to Apply: Prove it is unused (search, coverage, logs or metrics in production); delete it; run tests; keep the history in git.
Risks: Deleting code that is reached through reflection, config or external callers.
